575.title: The month of Poh
575.hook: in Poh the frost does not touch the one the Lord embraces (Barah Maha, ang 135)
575.howItsDone: On the Sangrand of Poh, many gurdwaras read the Poh stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; in the same season many Sikhs gather to remember Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade at Sirhind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maghar, and your line: maghar: sit together. Did you give someone ten quiet minutes? Sitting close was the first move against the cold. Today the cold arrives in full. Day five hundred seventy-five.

Anyone who has spent winter in a village in Punjab knows the fog. In Poh, roughly mid-December to mid-January, it can sit on the fields all day. The cold gets into the walls. People wrap themselves in heavy shawls, sit around small fires, and hand each other cups of tea with both hands. At the very end of the month comes Lohri, a bonfire night when families gather around the flames. Cold makes you notice warmth. It also makes you notice who is out in it. Guru Arjan's Poh stanza begins in the frost, and asks who it can't touch.
screen: `POH: FOG ON THE FIELDS ALL DAY.` → `SHAWLS, FIRES, TEA IN BOTH HANDS.` → `WHO CAN THE FROST NOT TOUCH?`

segments.voice: The stanza opens pokh tukhaar na vi-aapa-ee, kanth mili-aa har naahu. In paraphrase: in Poh, the frost does not touch the one whom the Lord, the Beloved, has embraced. Tukhaar is frost. Vi-aapa-ee means to seize, to get into you, the way cold gets into your bones. And kanth mili-aa is a hug, literally an arm around the neck. So the picture is plain and physical: the cold is real, and you are being held. The stanza goes on. The mind is pierced by love for the Lord's lotus feet, and fixed on the sight of Him. Take the shelter of the Lord of the world, it says, and serve the Master; that's the real profit. And it ends: in Poh, all comforts belong to the one whom the carefree Lord forgives. Notice what it doesn't promise. It doesn't say winter goes away. It says the frost doesn't seize the one who is embraced. That's a different kind of warmth, one that works inside the weather. For Sikhs, Poh carries a memory that makes this line hard and holy. In December, in the early 1700s, Mata Gujri, the mother of Guru Gobind Singh, and his two youngest sons were held at Sirhind in the cold, before the boys were executed. Tradition remembers they were kept in an open tower in the winter air, and that they did not give up their faith. Many Sikhs gather in Poh to remember them. Held warm, in the Barah Maha, has never meant nothing hard happens. It means you are not alone in the cold.
screen: `TUKHAAR: THE FROST THAT SEIZES.` · `KANTH MILI-AA: HELD IN AN EMBRACE.` · `THE WEATHER STAYS; THE COLD CAN'T SEIZE.` · `POH: SIKHS REMEMBER MATA GUJRI.` · then, large: `POH: HELD WARM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wrap up warm and give thanks. Take a blanket, a sweater, a scarf, or just your own arms around yourself. Sit and feel the warmth gather. Notice where it starts: shoulders, chest, hands. Then give thanks for it, plainly. For the roof, the cloth, the hands that made it. If you pray, you can thank Waheguru in your own words. If you don't, simply let gratitude sit in the warmth. And spare one breath for someone out in the cold tonight. The bell holds the time.
Poh. In the Barah Maha, Poh is the deep cold, and the frost cannot seize the one the Beloved holds in an embrace.

Your line: poh: held warm. Today, when something feels cold, a hard email, a lonely hour, remember the embrace the stanza describes. And if you can, be warmth for one person. Day five hundred seventy-five.

576.title: The month of Magh
576.hook: in Magh, bathe in the dust of the holy (Barah Maha, ang 135)
576.howItsDone: Sikhs mark the first of Magh as Maghi, and many bathe in the sarovar at Muktsar to remember the Forty Liberated; gurdwaras read Guru Arjan's Magh stanza, and serving the sangat, even cleaning shoes, is a common act of humility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Poh, and your line: poh: held warm. Did you wrap up, give thanks, and spare a thought for someone in the cold? Today, still in winter, the Barah Maha asks us to take a bath. Day five hundred seventy-six.

Cold water at dawn, in the middle of winter. In north India, Magh, roughly mid-January to mid-February, is a month of bathing: Hindu tradition prizes a dawn dip in a river in Magh as an act of devotion. Sikhs mark the month's first day with Maghi, and at Muktsar in Punjab people bathe in the sacred pool to remember the Forty Liberated, the Sikhs tradition says fell there in battle beside Guru Gobind Singh. So when Guru Arjan reached Magh in his Barah Maha, his listeners already had water on their minds. And the bath he describes isn't in a river at all.
screen: `MAGH: A MONTH OF BATHING.` → `MAGHI AT MUKTSAR.` → `A BATH, BUT NOT IN A RIVER.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens maagh majan sang saadhoo-aa, dhoorree kar isnaan. In paraphrase: in Magh, let your bathing be in the company of the holy; make their dust your bath. Majan is bathing. Isnaan is washing. And dhoorree is dust, the dust from the feet of the holy. It's a startling image. Dust is usually what a bath removes. But in Punjabi devotion, the dust of the feet is the sign of the lowest place. To touch it is to make yourself small, to say: I'll sit below you, I'll learn from you. So the bath that makes you clean, in this stanza, is humility. The stanza goes on: meditate on the Lord's Name, listen to it, and give it to everyone. Then the filth of past deeds washes off, and pride leaves the mind. And it says the merit of all the sixty-eight pilgrimage places is found in compassion for living beings. That's the turn. The stanza doesn't mock the river, or the people standing in it at dawn. It moves the bath. Wherever you are, you can bathe this way: sitting low among good people, hearing the Name, and being kind to anything alive. A Sikh habit catches this. In the gurdwara, people sit on the floor, often near the door where shoes are left, and volunteers clean those shoes for strangers as seva. It's the dust of the feet, made practical. Magh's bath ends where all baths end. You come out lighter. The stanza says it's pride you've washed off.
screen: `MAJAN: BATHE IN HOLY COMPANY.` · `DHOORREE: THE DUST OF THEIR FEET.` · `PRIDE WASHES OFF.` · `COMPASSION HOLDS THE PILGRIMAGE.` · then, large: `MAGH: HUMBLE BATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash your face mindfully. If you can, go to a sink now. If not, picture it. Feel the water's temperature on your hands first. Then bring it to your face, slowly. Notice the cool, the drip, the way the skin wakes up. As you dry your face, let go of one small pride you've been carrying today, being right, being busy, being better at something. Then sit for the rest of the time, face fresh, with one small pride set down. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Magh. In the Barah Maha, Magh's bath is taken in the company of the holy, in the dust of their feet, and it washes off pride.
Your line: magh: humble bath. Today, take one low place on purpose: listen instead of correcting, or tidy up after others without saying so. Day five hundred seventy-six.

577.title: The month of Phagun
577.hook: in Phagun bliss comes, the Friend revealed (Barah Maha, ang 136)
577.howItsDone: On the Sangrand of Phagun many gurdwaras read the Phagun stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; around the same season Sikhs gather at Anandpur Sahib for Hola Mohalla, begun by Guru Gobind Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Magh, and your line: magh: humble bath. Did you take one low place on purpose? Washed of pride, the bride reaches the last month of the year. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

There's a particular sound at an airport arrivals gate. Someone has been waiting a long time, checking the board, rereading the same text. Then the doors slide open, and they see the face. The sound they make isn't a word. It's half a laugh and half a cry, and everybody nearby turns and smiles. Phagun, roughly mid-February to mid-March, is when Punjab's winter breaks. Mustard is in flower, the days warm, and in the Barah Maha, after a year of longing, the doors finally open.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS GATE.` → `HALF A LAUGH, HALF A CRY.` → `PHAGUN: THE DOORS OPEN.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens phalgun anand upaarjanaa, har sajan pragate aa-e. In paraphrase: in Phagun, bliss springs up; the Lord, the Friend, has appeared. Anand is bliss, deep joy, the same word that names Guru Amar Das's hymn Anand Sahib. Upaarjanaa is to arise, to be produced. And sajan is a friend, a dear one, the word you'd use for someone you love. Pragate aa-e: has come, made visible. So after all those months of the Beloved being far, here He is, revealed. Notice who brings it about. The saints, the Lord's helpers, the stanza says, in their kindness have brought about the meeting. That's the holy company we met in Assu and Maghar, still at work. Then the stanza fills with celebration. The bed is beautiful, every comfort is here, and now there's no room for sorrow. Her wish is fulfilled. Friends gather and sing songs of joy, the songs of the Lord of the world. And then a quiet line: no one else like the Lord can be seen; there's no other to compare with Him. Phagun is a season of spring festivals. Around Holi, Sikhs gather at Anandpur Sahib for Hola Mohalla, which Sikh tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh. Color, music, a crowd. The Barah Maha's bliss isn't private. It's a party with friends. And there's a lesson in the order. Joy was already there in Chet, the first month, in remembering. But the meeting itself doesn't come first. It comes last, after doubt, longing, honesty and humility. The poem doesn't treat those months as wasted. They led here.
screen: `ANAND: BLISS SPRINGS UP.` · `SAJAN: THE FRIEND, REVEALED.` · `THE SAINTS BRING THE MEETING.` · `FRIENDS GATHER AND SING.` · then, large: `PHAGUN: BLISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: celebrate one small thing. Sit comfortably and look back over the last few days. Find one thing that went right, however small: a warm call, a good meal, a task finished, a moment of laughter. Let yourself actually enjoy it again, not just note it. Smile if you like. Then think who you could tell, because Phagun's joy is shared. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths, or hum a line of a shabad you love. The bell holds the time.
Phagun. In the Barah Maha, Phagun is the last month of the year and the month of meeting: bliss springs up, and the Friend is revealed.
Your line: phagun: bliss. Today, tell one person about one good thing, and let them be glad with you. Joy grows when it's shared. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

578.title: Every day is blessed
578.hook: the days, months and moments are blessed for those on whom grace falls (Barah Maha, ang 136)
578.howItsDone: On Sangrand, the first day of each solar month, many gurdwaras hold a special diwan where the new month's stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha is read; some Sikhs keep the day gladly, while others stress that the poem's closing makes every day equally blessed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Phagun, and your line: phagun: bliss. Did you share one good thing with someone? The year of the Barah Maha has turned all the way round. Today it closes, with one short stanza about every day there is. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

Which date to marry on? Which morning to sign the lease? Which hour to start the journey? Plenty of calendars mark some days as lucky and others as not. In Punjab, the first day of each solar month, when the sun moves into a new sign, is called Sangrand. On Sangrand many gurdwaras hold a special gathering, and the stanza of the Barah Maha for the new month is read aloud. So you might expect the poem to end by naming its best month. It doesn't.
screen: `WHICH DAYS ARE LUCKY?` → `SANGRAND: THE MONTH'S FIRST DAY.` → `THE POEM'S LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: The Barah Maha's closing stanza says, in paraphrase: the months, the days and the moments are blessed for those on whom the Lord casts His glance of grace. Nanak begs for the gift of Your sight; be merciful, Lord. Moorat, the word for moment, is the same word people use for an auspicious hour. And the stanza simply hands every hour to grace. No month in the poem is holy by itself. Chet isn't better than Poh. What makes a day blessed is whether it is lived in the Lord's sight. Sikhs hold Sangrand in two ways, and this stanza speaks to both. Many keep it gladly: a monthly gathering, a reason to come to the gurdwara, a chance to hear the new month's stanza and begin again. Some Sikhs are wary of Sangrand becoming a lucky day, and point to this closing to say that no date carries power of its own. Both are trying to honor the same line. Now look back at the whole poem. It began with a year of longing, and a bride separated by her own deeds. Chet brought joy in remembering. Vaisakh, longing. Jeth, bowing. Asarh, keeping Him near in the heat. Sawan, blossoming. Bhadon, doubt. Assu, how to meet. Katak, blaming no one. Maghar, sitting together. Poh, held warm. Magh, the humble bath. Phagun, bliss. Twelve moods of one heart. And the last stanza says that every one of them, even the doubt, can be a blessed month. Every month is His.
screen: `MONTHS, DAYS, MOMENTS: BLESSED BY GRACE.` · `NO MONTH IS HOLY BY ITSELF.` · `TWO WAYS TO KEEP SANGRAND.` · `TWELVE MOODS OF ONE HEART.` · then, large: `EVERY MONTH IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark the next Sangrand. Look up the date when the next Punjabi month begins, in a Sikh calendar or a gurdwara's notice, and put it in your diary. Write beside it the name of the month and its line from this block: Assu, how to meet; Poh, held warm; whichever comes next. Then sit with the breath, and let today count too, ordinary as it is. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Sangrand. The first day of a solar month, when gurdwaras read that month's stanza of the Barah Maha; and the poem's closing says every day is blessed when grace falls on it.

Your line: every month is his. Today, when you catch yourself calling it a bad day, add three words: still His day. Then see what changes. Tomorrow, a new voice: the ninth Guru. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

579.title: The ninth Guru's voice
579.hook: his hymns are short, calm and plain, about the passing world and the steady Name
579.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads, marked Mahalla 9, are sung in kirtan across many ragas, and his saloks are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sangrand, and your line: every month is his. Did you call a hard day still His day? The Barah Maha is finished. Today a new block begins, and a new voice. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

Sikh tradition tells this story. The boy Guru, Har Krishan, was dying in Delhi, and said only that the next Guru would be found at Bakala, a village in Punjab. Soon Bakala was full of men claiming to be Guru. Then a trader named Makhan Shah arrived. Caught in a storm at sea, he had vowed five hundred gold coins to the Guru if his ship survived. It had. So he went from claimant to claimant, laying two coins before each. Each one took them, pleased. At last he found a quiet man who had made no claim at all. That man looked up and asked about the rest of the promise.
screen: `BAKALA: MANY CLAIMANTS.` → `MAKHAN SHAH'S VOW.` → `THE QUIET MAN WHO MADE NO CLAIM.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Makhan Shah ran up to the rooftop shouting that he had found the Guru. The quiet man was Tegh Bahadur, youngest son of Guru Hargobind, and he became the ninth Guru. Tradition remembers long years he had spent at Bakala in meditation. That stillness is all over his hymns. Sikh tradition says his bani was added to the Granth by his son, Guru Gobind Singh. It's a short body of work next to Guru Arjan's: shabads spread through the ragas, and a run of saloks near the very end of the book. And it sounds different. Some readers hear his language leaning toward Braj, the old poetic speech of the region around Mathura, softer and more flowing than the Punjabi of the earlier Gurus. The hymns are short. They often begin by speaking straight to someone: saadho, holy ones, or man re, O mind. And they keep returning to two things. Everything we see is passing, like a dream or the shadow of a cloud. And the Name of the Lord is the one thing that stays. There's no anger in them. No fireworks. Just plain, calm sentences, the way an older friend talks to you when it matters. That calm wasn't a mood he had for poetry. Sikhs remember that he gave his life in Delhi, refusing to bow under force, and his hymns are the voice of the man who walked toward that. For the next month, we'll listen to it: a voice that doesn't raise itself, and is very hard to forget.
screen: `THE QUIET MAN BECAME THE NINTH GURU.` · `SHABADS AND SALOKS, ADDED BY HIS SON.` · `SAADHO, MAN RE: SPOKEN STRAIGHT.` · `PASSING WORLD, STEADY NAME.` · then, large: `CALM AND PLAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one of his shabads. If you can, find a recording of a shabad by Guru Tegh Bahadur, marked Mahalla nine, and play it now, eyes closed. Don't work at the meaning. Just listen to the pace of it, the plainness. If you can't play anything, sit quietly and imagine a voice that never hurries, saying something true. Notice what your own breath does when nothing is shouting at it. The bell holds the time.
Shabad, a hymn, the Guru's word. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns are short, calm and plain: the passing world, and the steady Name.
Your line: calm and plain. Today, in one conversation that matters, try saying the true thing simply and slowly, without raising your voice to make it land. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

580.title: Give up pride, holy ones
580.hook: saadho man kaa maan tiaago: holy ones, give up the mind's pride (Gauri M9, ang 219)
580.tomorrow: The world as a wall of sand
580.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabad 'saadho man kaa maan tiaago' in Raag Gauri in kirtan, and many hear it as a reminder that pride is the danger of the devout.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shabad, and your line: calm and plain. Did you say one true thing simply, without raising your voice? Today we hear that voice speak its first line to us. Day five hundred eighty.

Here's a test anyone can run. Next time someone corrects you in front of other people, even about something tiny, the spelling of a name, the year a film came out, watch what happens inside. There's a flash of heat. A quick story about why you were actually right, or why it doesn't matter, or why they're being annoying. It takes about half a second. That flash is pride, and it guards the mind like a bouncer at a door. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Raag Gauri begins by speaking straight to the people who think they're past all that.
screen: `CORRECTED IN FRONT OF OTHERS.` → `A FLASH OF HEAT.` → `PRIDE GUARDS THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens saadho man kaa maan tiaago. Holy ones, give up the mind's pride. Listen to the sounds: man is the mind, and maan is pride, honor, self-regard. Man kaa maan, the mind's maan. The two words nearly rhyme, as if pride were the mind's shadow, following it everywhere. And notice who he's talking to: saadho, holy ones, the good and devout. Pride can grow quietly in good people, because they have real things to be proud of. In paraphrase, the hymn goes on. Run day and night from lust, from anger, and from bad company. The one who knows pleasure and pain as the same, and honor and dishonor too, who stays beyond joy and grief, has understood the essence of the world. Leave both praise and blame, it says, and seek the state of freedom. Then the last line, in paraphrase: this is a hard game, says Nanak; only a few, turned toward the Guru, understand it. That's an honest ending. He doesn't pretend it's easy. Giving up pride isn't a one-time decision. It's more like a game you keep playing, round after round, every time the flash of heat comes. And here's the turn in the hymn: pride and honor are the same word, maan. The pride he asks us to drop is the need to be honored. Let that go, and dishonor loses its sting. Someone corrects you, and it's just information. That's the freedom the hymn is pointing at.
screen: `MAN KAA MAAN: THE MIND'S PRIDE.` · `SPOKEN TO THE HOLY ONES.` · `HONOR AND DISHONOR, THE SAME.` · `A HARD GAME, PLAYED ROUND BY ROUND.` · then, large: `GIVE UP THE PRIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one proud thought. Sit comfortably and breathe slowly. Let the mind go wherever it likes, and watch for a thought that puffs you up: I'm better at this than them, they should have asked me, I deserve more credit. When one comes, don't argue with it. Just notice it, name it, pride, and set it down, the way you'd put down a heavy bag. If another comes, do the same. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Maan, the mind's pride, the need to be honored. Guru Tegh Bahadur tells even the holy ones to let go of it. He calls it a hard game.
Your line: give up the pride. Today, when someone corrects you, feel the flash of heat, then say thank you and mean it. One round of the hard game. Day five hundred eighty.

581.title: The world as a wall of sand
581.hook: saadho rachnaa raam banaaee: this creation the Lord made is passing like a dream (Gauri M9, ang 219)
581.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's Gauri shabad 'saadho rachnaa raam banaaee' in kirtan, and often hear his images of the dream, the cloud's shadow and the wall of sand as reminders to hold the world lightly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maan, and your line: give up the pride. Did you thank someone who corrected you? This week went from Poh's warmth and Magh's bath to Phagun's bliss and every month being His, then into the ninth Guru's calm voice. Today, that voice looks at the world itself. Day five hundred eighty-one.

On a beach in summer, a child builds a castle. Towers, a moat, a wall, a shell on top for a flag. It takes all afternoon, and the child is completely serious about it. Then the tide comes in. Some kids cry. Some kids shriek with delight and run to build again. The adults watching smile, because they know something the child is only learning: the wall was never going to last. Guru Tegh Bahadur reaches for a picture like this one: a wall of sand. And then he asks a harder question: what are we building that's any different?
screen: `A SANDCASTLE, BUILT ALL AFTERNOON.` → `THE TIDE COMES IN.` → `WHAT ARE WE BUILDING?`

segments.voice: His hymn in Raag Gauri opens saadho rachnaa raam banaaee. Holy ones, this creation the Lord has made. Then, in paraphrase: one person perishes, and another thinks he will stay forever; it's a wonder that can't be described. Gripped by lust, anger and attachment, people forget the Lord. They take the body to be permanent, when it's like a dream that comes in the night. Whatever is seen will pass, like the shadow of a cloud. And the last line, in paraphrase: Nanak has known the world as mithiaa, false, not lasting, and stays in the Lord's shelter. Look at the two pictures. A dream at night feels completely real while you're in it. A cloud's shadow crosses a field and is gone before you can walk to it. The wall of sand, baaloo kee bheet, is the image he uses elsewhere, in a salok we'll reach later in this block. It's the same thought in a third picture: carefully built, and not built to last. Now, the hymn isn't sneering at the world. It also calls it rachnaa raam banaaee, the creation the Lord made. Some readers hear mithiaa, false, as false to lean on, because it won't last. What the Guru points at is our mistake: treating the sandcastle as if it were bedrock, then breaking our hearts when the tide comes. Think back over this week. Poh's warmth, Magh's bath, Phagun's bliss: none of those months stayed. Each passed into the next. And the closing of the Barah Maha said every one of them was blessed anyway. Passing doesn't mean worthless. It means hold it like sand, gently, with open hands.
screen: `RACHNAA: THE CREATION THE LORD MADE.` · `A DREAM IN THE NIGHT.` · `A CLOUD'S SHADOW ON A FIELD.` · `HOLD IT LIKE SAND.` · then, large: `PASSING, LIKE A DREAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch sand or water move. If you can, pour a little water slowly from one glass to another, or let sand or sugar run through your fingers. If not, picture a river, or the sand in an hourglass. Watch it keep moving. Nothing in the stream stays still, and yet the stream is there. Breathe with it. Let one thing you've been gripping too tightly loosen, just a little. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Rachnaa, the creation, what the Lord has made. In Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, it is passing, like a dream, a cloud's shadow, a wall of sand.
Your line: passing, like a dream. Today, when something goes wrong that you'd built carefully, try saying the line once, then pick up the next handful of sand. Day five hundred eighty-one.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rachnaa, creation, what is made. The hymn calls the world the rachnaa the Lord made.

what a scholar hears: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns return again and again to a small set of images, the dream, the cloud's shadow, the wall of sand, so the same lesson lands in plain, repeated pictures.
